title: Artificial intelligence governance: Ethical considerations and implications for social responsibility
explain_beginner: The paper looks at how artificial intelligence should be managed responsibly. It reviews rules and guidance from large tech companies, governments, and international groups. It also connects these rules with the idea that organizations owe duties to customers and society. The author highlights important areas: being able to explain how AI works, checking results can be repeated, treating people fairly, including diverse users, protecting privacy and safety, and reducing risks and cyber threats. The main message is that everyone who builds, studies, or maintains AI has ethical and social duties to consumers and other people affected. Why matters: AI affects people, so responsibility matters.
explain_business: For executives, this paper suggests that artificial intelligence needs clear oversight, not just technical performance. It reviews guidance from major technology companies, governments, and international bodies, then identifies practical areas leaders should manage: explaining decisions, repeating results, fair treatment, inclusion, privacy, safety, and reducing risk and security threats. The paper also says everyone involved in building, researching, or maintaining these systems has social and moral obligations to customers and society. This informs decisions about oversight policies, evidence requests, and who is accountable when AI affects people. It supports making these obligations part of how AI is managed.
explain_practitioner: This study responds to a shortage of work on principles and rules for people who build expert systems such as machine learning and deep learning. It examines frameworks proposed by large technology firms, government policy bodies, and international organizations. It also reviews existing writing on managing artificial intelligence and on how that connects with companies' social duties. From this, it names several important areas: clear responsibility and openness, understandable and repeatable systems, fair and inclusive treatment, user privacy and safety, and prevention of risks and security problems. The key result is that researchers, developers, and maintainers all carry social and moral obligations toward consumers and wider society.
